mainTopic: Whether a person may injure himself, payment for taking away someone's מצוה, and when fruit trees may be cut down.
overview: The גמרא first finishes a question on רבי עקיבא's words. It explains that a person may shame himself but may not injure himself, and others who do either to him must pay. Next, a ברייתא about a שבועה to harm oneself seems to show that self-injury is allowed. שמואל says that oath means an oath to fast, and the גמרא defends this by saying you can make others fast by locking them up. A second ברייתא shows the oath is about real injury, so the גמרא concludes that the question is a מחלוקת תנאים. It then searches for the תנא who forbids self-injury. It rejects רבי אלעזר's teachings about one's own blood and about tearing clothes over the dead, and settles on רבי אלעזר הקפר, who calls a נזיר a sinner for giving up wine. Next, רב reads a ברייתא that frees a damager who says 'you told me to' as being about an ox or tree that was going to be destroyed anyway. In that case the owner's claim is that he lost the chance to do the מצוה himself, as רבן גמליאל ruled about כיסוי הדם. The amud ends with rules about cutting down fruit trees: how much fruit protects a tree, when the wood's value permits cutting it, and that barren trees should be cut first.

steps.title: The challenge from רבי עקיבא's own words
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its challenge: רבי עקיבא described the man as one who 'injures himself, though not permitted,' which seems to fit humiliation too.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי עקיבא taught: one who injures himself, even though he is not allowed to, is exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing a challenge that began just before this point. It quotes רבי עקיבא's statement as proof that a person may not even shame himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story was about בושת (humiliation), yet רבי עקיבא used the phrase 'not permitted.' So it seems he holds that a person may not humiliate himself either. That clashes with the idea that a person may shame himself.

phrases.english: And it teaches: one who injures himself,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי – פָּטוּר!
phrases.english: even though he is not permitted, is exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְקָתָנֵי: הַחוֹבֵל בְּעַצְמוֹ, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי – פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a challenge that started in the text before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a person may humiliate himself.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי עקיבא applied 'not permitted' in a story about humiliation, which suggests self-humiliation is forbidden too.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא was arguing from the stronger case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי עקיבא meant: others are surely liable for בושת, since they are liable even for חבלה, where a person may not hurt himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he meant: no need to say this about humiliation, where a person may shame himself. Even for injury, where a person may not injure himself, others who injure him must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by rereading רבי עקיבא's words. The phrase 'not permitted' was about injury, not about humiliation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא used a 'not only this, but even that' argument. With injury, the person himself is not allowed to do it, and others still pay. With shaming, the person is allowed to shame himself, but others who shame him are certainly liable. So the 'not permitted' line never applied to בושת.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he said to him (this is what he meant)
It is not needed to say

steps.whatToRemember: A person may shame himself but may not injure himself. Others who do either one to him must pay.

phrases.english: This is what he said to him:
It is not necessary to say regarding humiliation,
where a person is permitted to humiliate himself;
but even regarding injury,
where a person is not permitted to injure himself –
others who injured him are liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the statement as a 'not only this, but even that' argument
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא's 'not permitted' was about humiliation too, so a person may not shame himself.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Not permitted' applies only to injury. A person may shame himself, and others who shame him are liable all the more.

steps.title: A ברייתא suggests harming yourself is allowed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the rule that a person may not injure himself, using a ברייתא that counts an oath to harm oneself as an oath about something allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is a person really not allowed to injure himself? A ברייתא teaches: you might think someone who swore to harm himself and did not do it is exempt. The פסוק says 'to do evil or to do good.' Just as doing good means something optional, doing evil also means something optional. So I include one who swore to harm himself and did not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now attacks the rule just stated, that a person may not injure himself. It brings a ברייתא about a שבועת ביטוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person is liable for breaking an oath only if the oath was about something optional (רשות), not something already forbidden. The ברייתא says an oath to harm oneself does make him liable. That means harming oneself counts as optional, so it should be allowed.
steps.confusionAlert: Being 'liable' here is a good sign for the act. It means the oath was valid because the act was optional, not forbidden.

phrases.english: And is a person not permitted to injure himself?
But it was taught: One might think, if one swore to do harm to himself –
and did not do harm, he would be exempt?
phrases.notes: Exempt from bringing the קרבן for a broken oath.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "To do evil or to do good" –
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:4

phrases.english: just as doing good is an optional matter,
so too doing evil is an optional matter;

phrases.aramaic: אָבִיא נִשְׁבָּע לְהָרַע בְּעַצְמוֹ וְלֹא הֵרַע!
phrases.english: I will include one who swore to harm himself and did not harm!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין אָדָם רַשַּׁאי לְחַבֵּל בְּעַצְמוֹ? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule stated in step 2 that self-injury is forbidden.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a person may not injure himself.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Oaths count only for optional acts. The ברייתא treats harming oneself as a valid oath, so harming oneself must be optional (allowed).

steps.title: שמואל: the oath was to fast
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that the ברייתא is not about injuring oneself, but about an oath to fast, which is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: it means someone who swore, 'I will sit in a fast.'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the challenge by narrowing what 'harm to himself' means in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fasting causes a person discomfort, so it counts as 'harm,' but it is allowed. So the ברייתא never says physical injury is optional. The rule against injuring oneself stands.

keyTerms.meaning: I will sit in a fast (I will fast)

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
It refers to one who says: "I will sit in a fast."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's 'harm to himself' includes physical injury, so injuring oneself is allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means fasting, which is allowed. Physical self-injury is still forbidden.

steps.title: Can you make others fast?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: the matching case in the ברייתא, harming others, would then mean making others fast, and that is impossible.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then the matching case of harming others would mean making them sit in a fast. Can a person make others sit in a fast?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on שמואל's answer by checking whether it also works for the other half of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same ברייתא also speaks about an oath to harm others, which is forbidden and so does not create a valid oath. If 'harm' means fasting for oneself, then 'harm to others' should mean making others fast. But you cannot force other people to fast, so that reading seems strange.

phrases.english: The matching case regarding harming others –
would be to make them sit in a fast;
can one make others sit in a fast?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's answer in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's reading that 'harm' in the ברייתא means fasting.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's parallel case of harming others would then have to mean making others fast, which a person cannot do.

steps.title: You can make others fast by locking them up
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that making others fast is possible: a person can lock them in a room so they cannot get food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, it is possible: for example, where he locks them up in a room.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל. It shows that an oath to make others fast does make sense, because you can lock people in a room.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge in Step 5 said 'making others fast' is impossible, so שמואל's reading could not fit the matching case of harming others. The גמרא answers that a person can stop others from getting food by shutting them in. So the pair still works: an oath to fast yourself, and an oath to make others fast.

keyTerms.meaning: Where he locks them up or shuts them in

phrases.english: Yes; where he locks them up
in a room.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 5 and defends שמואל's reading.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical case definition: shows the case the challenger thought impossible can really happen.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Making another person fast is impossible, so שמואל's reading breaks down for 'harming others.'
steps.terutzMaskana: A person can make others fast by locking them in a room, so שמואל's reading still works.

steps.title: A ברייתא defines harming others as physical injury
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל from a ברייתא that defines 'harming others' as hitting someone and splitting his head, which is real injury, not fasting.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught in a ברייתא: What counts as an oath to harm others? 'I will strike so-and-so and crack his skull.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא showing that 'harming others' means physically hurting them. That undoes שמואל's idea that the oath is about fasting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'harming others' means real injury, then 'harming oneself' in the same ברייתא must also mean real injury. That ברייתא calls such an oath one about something allowed. So the ברייתא does treat self-injury as permitted, and that clashes with רבי עקיבא's rule that a person may not injure himself.

keyTerms.meaning: I will wound his brain (crack his skull)

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: What is harming others?
"I will strike so-and-so and wound his brain"!
phrases.notes: This is real physical injury, not fasting. So 'harming oneself' in the matching case must also mean injury.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Even after Step 6 defended שמואל, this ברייתא shows the case really is about physical injury.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's explanation (Step 4) that the oath to harm oneself means an oath to fast.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא defines harming others as physical injury. So the matching 'harming oneself' must be injury too, and the ברייתא treats it as allowed. That brings back the clash with the rule that a person may not injure himself.

steps.title: It is a disagreement among תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that there is no single answer: some תנאים say a person may not injure himself, and some say he may.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is a disagreement among תנאים. One תנא says a person may not injure himself, and one תנא says a person may injure himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the attempt to make both sources agree. It says they reflect two different opinions among the תנאים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of explaining away the ברייתא, the גמרא accepts that it holds self-injury is permitted. רבי עקיבא in our משנה holds it is forbidden. The two sources simply follow opposing views.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a disagreement among תנאים

steps.whatToRemember: Whether a person may injure himself is a מחלוקת תנאים. רבי עקיבא forbids it, and the ברייתא about oaths permits it.

phrases.english: Rather, it is a dispute of תנאים;
for there is one who says:
a person is not permitted to injure himself,
and there is one who says:
a person is permitted to injure himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of Step 7 and settles the clash by assigning the two sources to different תנאים.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מחלוקת תנאים: the two sources follow opposing opinions.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All sources must agree, so the ברייתא has to be reinterpreted (as שמואל tried).
steps.terutzMaskana: The sources disagree. One opinion forbids self-injury and another permits it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next search: which תנא actually holds that self-injury is forbidden.

steps.title: Which תנא forbids self-injury?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who the תנא is that holds a person may not injure himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who is the תנא you have heard say that a person may not injure himself?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now looks for the source of the opinion that forbids self-injury. This question sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 said one תנא forbids self-injury and another permits it. The גמרא now wants a known ברייתא that shows the forbidding opinion.

phrases.english: Who is the תנא whom you heard say:
a person is not permitted to injure himself?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on Step 8 by asking for the source of the forbidding opinion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא's teaching shows the view that a person may not injure himself.

steps.title: First suggestion: רבי אלעזר on 'your blood'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests it is רבי אלעזר, who reads the פסוק as saying God will hold a person responsible for his own blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is this תנא, as it was taught: 'And surely your blood of your souls will I require.' רבי אלעזר says: From your own hand I will require your blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a first answer: maybe the תנא is רבי אלעזר. He learns from a פסוק that a person is punished for taking his own life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר reads 'from your souls' as 'from you yourselves.' So a person is held responsible even for shedding his own blood. The word אילימא tells us this is only a suggestion, and the גמרא may well reject it.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a suggestion that often gets rejected)
I will demand, I will hold accountable
From the hand of your souls, from yourselves

steps.confusionAlert: This is only a suggestion. אילימא usually means the גמרא is about to push back, so do not treat this as the final answer.

phrases.english: If you say it is this תנא –
as it was taught: "And surely your blood of your souls will I require" –
phrases.notes: בראשית 9:5

phrases.english: רבי אלעזר says:
From the hand of your souls I will require your blood;
phrases.notes: He means from your own hand. A person is held responsible even for taking his own life.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a first answer to the question of Step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A suggested answer: רבי אלעזר, who learns from בראשית 9:5 that a person is responsible for his own blood. It is offered with אילימא as a suggestion only.

steps.title: Killing may be different from injuring
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from רבי אלעזר: his פסוק may only forbid taking one's own life, not injuring oneself.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe killing is different!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion from step 10. רבי אלעזר's פסוק may only be talking about killing oneself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר's פסוק speaks about one's own blood, meaning suicide. Killing is far more severe than a wound, so a ban on killing oneself does not prove a ban on hurting oneself. The search for the right תנא must continue.

keyTerms.meaning: But maybe (a standard word for rejecting a proof)

phrases.english: But maybe killing is different!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the identification of the תנא proposed in step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using רבי אלעזר's reading of the פסוק about one's own blood as a source for a ban on self-injury.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The פסוק may cover only killing oneself, which is more severe than injury.

steps.title: Second try: tearing clothes too much over the dead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the תנא is רבי אלעזר, who says one who tears his clothes too much over a dead person gets lashes for בל תשחית. All the more so would this apply to his own body.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is this תנא, as a ברייתא teaches: one may tear clothes over the dead, and it is not a non-Jewish practice. רבי אלעזר said: I heard that one who tears too much over the dead gets lashes for 'do not destroy.' All the more so his own body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new answer to the question of step 9. רבי אלעזר says that wasting clothing by tearing it too much is forbidden, and the גמרא reasons that harming one's body must be even worse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time the source deals with destroying something, not with killing. Tearing clothes too much breaks the law of בל תשחית, the ban on needless destruction. The גמרא then argues upward: if wasting a garment is forbidden, damaging one's own body surely is.

keyTerms.meaning: Tearing one's clothes in mourning over a dead person
Forbidden practices of the non-Jewish nations

phrases.english: Rather, it is this תנא,
as it was taught: One may tear clothes over the dead,
and it is not one of the ways of the Emorites.
phrases.notes: This means it is a proper Jewish practice, not a forbidden non-Jewish custom.

phrases.english: רבי אלעזר said: I heard
that one who tears over the dead more than is fitting
gets lashes because of "do not destroy."
phrases.notes: דברים 20:19

phrases.english: And all the more so his own body.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הַאי תַּנָּא הוּא – דְּתַנְיָא: מְקָרְעִין עַל הַמֵּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 11 rejected the first answer, this offers a new candidate תנא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אלעזר, who forbids destroying clothes by tearing them too much. A ban on harming one's body would follow from this by a קל וחומר.

steps.title: Clothes may be different because they do not heal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the second answer. Ruining clothes is a permanent loss, while a body heals. רבי יוחנן and רב חסדא show how highly clothes were valued.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe clothes are different, because their loss never comes back! This is like רבי יוחנן, who called his clothes 'the things that honor me.' It is also like רב חסדא, who lifted his clothes when walking among thorns and said: 'This (my skin) heals, but this (my garment) does not heal.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the proof from tearing clothes. Damage to clothing is permanent, but the body can recover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'all the more so' from step 12 only works if the body is more precious than clothes. Here the גמרא points out that in one way clothes are more fragile, because a tear never repairs itself. רב חסדא even let his skin get scratched to protect his clothes. So a ban on ruining clothes does not prove a ban on injuring oneself.

keyTerms.meaning: A loss that does not come back (a permanent loss)
"The things that honor me" (רבי יוחנן's name for his clothes)

steps.confusionAlert: רב חסדא is not saying skin is worth less than clothing. He means that a scratch heals by itself, while a torn garment stays torn.

phrases.english: But maybe clothes are different,
since it is a loss that does not come back!
Like that of רבי יוחנן,
who called his clothes "the things that honor me,"
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and רב חסדא, when he would walk
among thorns and shrubs,
phrases.notes: Some versions read the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. The meaning is the same.

phrases.english: would lift up his clothes.
He said: This heals,
phrases.notes: "This" is his skin, and "this" in the next line is his garment.

phrases.english: but this does not heal.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא בְּגָדִים שָׁאנֵי, דִּפְסֵידָא דְּלָא הָדַר הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'all the more so' reasoning of step 12.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects learning a ban on self-injury from רבי אלעזר's ban on tearing clothes too much.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The קל וחומר fails, because clothes suffer permanent loss while the body heals.

steps.title: Final answer: רבי אלעזר הקפר and the נזיר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא settles on רבי אלעזר הקפר. He says a נזיר is called a sinner just for denying himself wine. By a קל וחומר, anyone who makes himself suffer in every way is surely a sinner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is this תנא, as a ברייתא teaches: רבי אלעזר הקפר ברבי said: Why does the verse say about a נזיר, 'he shall atone for him for sinning against the soul'? Against which soul did he sin? Rather, he sinned by making himself suffer without wine. Now reason it out: if this person, who only denied himself wine, is called a sinner, then one who denies himself everything is surely a sinner!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final source for the view that a person may not harm himself. A נזיר must bring a קרבן to atone for the suffering he caused himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This source is about causing oneself suffering, not about killing and not about property. The earlier objections therefore do not apply. If even the mild self-denial of giving up wine counts as a sin, then harming or afflicting oneself more seriously is surely forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the verse come to teach?
Reasoning from a lighter case to a stronger one

steps.whatToRemember: The תנא who forbids harming oneself is רבי אלעזר הקפר. If a נזיר is a 'sinner' just for giving up wine, then anyone who makes himself suffer is surely a sinner.
steps.whyThisMatters: This source gives a clear basis for the idea that a person's body is not his to harm freely, and that even needless self-denial can count as a sin.

phrases.english: Rather, it is this תנא, as it was taught:
רבי אלעזר הקפר ברבי said:
What does the verse come to teach when it says:
"And he shall atone for him for sinning against the soul"?
phrases.notes: במדבר 6:11. The verse is about a נזיר.

phrases.english: Against which soul did this person sin?
Rather, it is that he made himself suffer by keeping away from wine.
And can we not reason with a קל וחומר?
If this one, who made himself suffer
only by giving up wine, is called a sinner,
then one who makes himself suffer by giving up everything
how much more so is he a sinner!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הַאי תַּנָּא הוּא – דְּתַנְיָא: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר הַקַּפָּר בְּרַבִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 13 rejected the second answer, this gives a third candidate תנא, and the גמרא accepts it.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אלעזר הקפר, who calls a נזיר a sinner for denying himself wine. A ban on all self-affliction and self-harm follows from this by a קל וחומר.

steps.title: The ברייתא: 'You told me to do it' makes the damager exempt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about cutting saplings. Then רבה בר בר חנה teaches a ברייתא before רב: a damager who claims the owner told him to kill the ox or cut the trees is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One who cuts down his own saplings, etc.' רבה בר בר חנה taught this before רב: If the owner says, 'You killed my ox' or 'You cut down my saplings,' and the other says, 'You told me to kill it' or 'You told me to cut them down,' the other is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic from the משנה about saplings. It brings a ברייתא saying that a damager who claims 'you told me to' does not pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner claims damages, and the damager does not deny doing the act. He only claims he had permission. The ברייתא says that claim is enough to make him פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: Before רב, in front of רב
Exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.english: One who cuts down his own saplings, etc.

phrases.aramaic: תָּנֵי רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חַנָּה קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב:
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana taught before Rav:
'You killed my ox,' or 'You cut down my saplings';
and he answers, 'You told me to kill it,'
or 'You told me to cut them down': he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חַנָּה קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section of the משנה, separate from the discussion of injuring oneself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A damager who claims the owner told him to kill the ox or cut the trees is פטור.

steps.title: רב objects: this would let every damager go free
steps.stepSummary: רב attacks the ברייתא. If a damager can be פטור just by saying 'you told me to,' nobody will ever pay for damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said to him: If so, you leave no creature alive! Is it in his power to free himself just by saying this?
steps.whatsHappening: רב challenges the ברייתא that was just taught. He says it cannot be right as it stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Any damager could make up the claim 'you told me to,' so the ברייתא would wipe out all damage payments. רב also asks why the damager should be believed at all.

keyTerms.meaning: You leave no life for people; you destroy everyone
Is it in his power? Can he just say that?

phrases.english: He said to him: If so,
you leave no creature alive!
phrases.notes: He means: every damager will just say 'you told me to,' and no owner will ever get paid.

phrases.english: Is it in his power?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִם כֵּן, לָא שְׁבַקְתְּ חַיֵּי לְבִרְיָיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of the ברייתא in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that 'you told me to' makes the damager פטור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If an unproven claim of permission frees a damager, every damager will use it, and no one will ever pay.

steps.title: Should I erase the ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה asks רב whether he should remove this ברייתא from what he teaches.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Should I erase it?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנה asks a practical question after רב's attack: should he stop teaching this ברייתא?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רב showed the ברייתא leads to a bad result, it seems it may be a mistake. The question sets up רב's answer.

phrases.english: He said to him: Shall I erase it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רב's objection by asking if the ברייתא should be dropped.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the ברייתא should be removed from what is taught.

steps.title: רב: Keep it, but read it as an ox or tree that was going to be destroyed anyway
steps.stepSummary: רב says not to erase it. Instead, read the ברייתא as talking about an ox that was set to be killed, or a tree that was set to be cut down.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: No. Explain your ברייתא as talking about an ox that is standing to be killed, and a tree that is standing to be cut down.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers his own objection. He narrows the ברייתא to a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ox or tree was already going to be destroyed, it makes sense that the owner may have told him to do it. So the damager's claim is believable, and other damagers cannot use this excuse.
steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying the damager is always believed. The ברייתא now only applies when the ox or tree was going to be destroyed anyway.

phrases.english: He said to him: No;
explain your baraita as talking about an ox that is set to be killed,
and a tree that is set to be cut down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17 and solves the problem raised in step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא frees any damager who says 'you told me to.'
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only deals with an ox or tree that was already going to be destroyed, so the claim is believable.

steps.title: If it was going to be destroyed anyway, what is the owner complaining about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the ox or tree was going to be destroyed anyway, the owner lost nothing. So why is he suing at all?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is he claiming from him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's answer. In his case, it seems the owner has no loss to claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's answer fixed one problem but made a new one. If the ox or tree was going to be destroyed anyway, the owner did not lose anything, so why would he sue?

keyTerms.meaning: If so, if that is the case
What is he claiming from him?

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, מַאי קָא טָעֵין לֵיהּ?
phrases.english: If so, what is he claiming from him?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מַאי קָא טָעֵין לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's reading of the ברייתא in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's reading that the ox or tree was set to be destroyed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If it was going to be destroyed anyway, the owner lost nothing, so the lawsuit makes no sense.

steps.title: The owner wanted to do the מצוה himself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the owner claims he wanted to do the מצוה himself, and the other man took it from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He says to him: I wanted to do this מצוה myself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the owner lost. He lost the chance to do the מצוה of destroying the ox or tree himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if the ox or tree has no money value to him, the owner can still complain that his מצוה was taken. This explains why there is a lawsuit in רב's case.

phrases.english: Where he says to him:
I wanted to do this מצוה myself.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנָא בָּעֵינָא לְמִיעְבַּד הָא מִצְוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner lost nothing, so he has no claim.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner's claim is that he lost the chance to do the מצוה himself.

steps.title: Proof: רבן גמליאל fined someone for taking another's מצוה of covering blood
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: the one who slaughters should cover the blood. When someone else jumped ahead and covered it, רבן גמליאל made him pay ten gold coins.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'He shall pour out and cover': the one who poured out the blood should cover it. There was a story with someone who slaughtered, and another person jumped ahead and covered the blood, and רבן גמליאל made him pay ten gold coins.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves that taking away someone's מצוה is a real loss you can be made to pay for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links pouring and covering, so the מצוה of כיסוי הדם belongs to the one who slaughtered. רבן גמליאל made the one who took it pay, so the owner of the ox or tree can also claim for his lost מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: The מצוה of covering the blood of a slaughtered wild animal or bird

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא of 'you told me to' only deals with an ox or tree that was set to be destroyed. The owner's claim is for losing the מצוה, and רבן גמליאל shows that taking someone's מצוה can cost money.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a מצוה is treated as something of value that belongs to a person, and taking it away can lead to a payment.

phrases.english: As it was taught: 'He shall pour out and cover':
phrases.notes: ויקרא 17:13

phrases.english: the one who poured out the blood should cover it.
And there was a story with someone who slaughtered,
and another person jumped ahead and covered the blood,
and Rabban Gamliel made him liable
to give him ten gold coins.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 20 that losing a מצוה is a real claim.
steps.raayaObject: That a person can claim payment for having his מצוה taken from him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about כיסוי הדם and the ruling of רבן גמליאל, who made the one who took the מצוה pay ten gold coins.

steps.title: A palm tree that still gives a קב may not be cut down
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a palm tree still producing a קב of dates is forbidden to cut down.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: A palm tree that still produces a קב of fruit may not be cut down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling from רב about cutting down fruit trees. A palm tree that still gives a קב of fruit is protected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sets a minimum amount of fruit. Once a palm tree gives at least a קב, it still counts as a working fruit tree, and cutting it is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A קב, a measure of volume

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the starting rule for the איסור of destroying fruit trees, which the rest of this section develops.

phrases.english: Rav said:
A palm tree that bears a kav
phrases.notes: He means it still produces at least a קב of dates.

phrases.english: – it is forbidden to cut it down.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the topic of damaging plants and מצוות to a new ruling about when a fruit tree may not be cut down.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A palm tree producing a קב of fruit may not be cut down.

steps.title: An olive tree is protected at only a רובע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב from a source that protects an olive tree with only a רובע of fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: How much fruit must be on an olive tree so that one may not cut it down? A quarter-קב!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב. A source says an olive tree is protected even with only a quarter-קב of fruit, much less than רב's full קב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a quarter-קב is enough to protect a tree, why does רב need a full קב? The two amounts seem to clash.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
How much must be on an olive tree
so that one may not cut it down?
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is the corrected wording, making it read 'cut it down.'

phrases.english: A quarter-kav!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: כַּמָּה יְהֵא בַּזַּיִת וְלֹא יִקְצְצֶנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's amount of a קב from step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that a tree needs a קב of fruit to be protected.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A source protects an olive tree at only a רובע, so a full קב seems too high a minimum.

steps.title: Olive trees are more valuable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that olive trees are different because they are more significant.
steps.simpleTranslation: Olive trees are different, because they are valuable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. Olive trees are special and valuable, so even a small amount of fruit protects them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two amounts do not clash. A palm needs a קב, but an olive tree is worth so much that even a רובע of olives makes it worth keeping.

phrases.english: Olive trees are different,
since they are significant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: olive trees have a lower minimum because they are more valuable.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One amount should apply to all fruit trees, so רב's קב contradicts the רובע.
steps.terutzMaskana: Olive trees are protected at a רובע because of their value; other trees like palms need a קב.

steps.title: רבי חנינא's son died for cutting a fig tree too early
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא says his son שבחת died only because he cut down a fig tree before its time.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: My son שבחת died only because he cut down a fig tree before its time.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא shares a personal story showing how serious it is to cut down a fruit tree too early.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a new measurement but a warning. It shows that cutting a fruit tree while it still gives fruit carries a heavy punishment.

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said:
My son Shivchat did not die
except because he cut down a fig tree
before its time.
phrases.notes: Meaning while it was still producing fruit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: לָא שְׁכֵיב שִׁיבְחַת בְּרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a story that stresses how serious the rule of step 22 is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cutting a fruit tree before its time is dangerous and was punished with death.

steps.title: If the wood is worth more, cutting is allowed
steps.stepSummary: רבינא says that if the tree is worth more as wood than for its fruit, it may be cut down.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: But if it was worth more money, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא adds a limit to the איסור. If cutting the tree is worth more money than keeping it for its fruit, it is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The איסור is about destroying something useful. If the wood brings in more than the fruit would, cutting the tree is not a loss, so it is permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This becomes a key practical rule: cutting a fruit tree is allowed when keeping it would be the bigger loss.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
But if it was worth more in money,
phrases.notes: He means the tree is worth more as wood than for its fruit.

phrases.english: it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבִינָא: וְאִם הָיָה מְעוּלֶּה בְּדָמִים, מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the איסור of steps 22 and 25 with an exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fruit tree worth more as wood than for its fruit may be cut down.

steps.title: A ברייתא reads the פסוק as allowing even a fruit tree
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that reads 'רק עץ אשר תדע' as a fruit tree and 'כי לא עץ מאכל הוא' as a barren tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: 'Only the tree that you know' — this is a fruit tree. 'That it is not a food tree' — this is a barren tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support רבינא. It reads the פסוק as allowing, in some cases, even a fruit tree to be cut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק that permits cutting has two parts. The ברייתא says one part refers to a fruit tree, which shows there is a case where cutting a fruit tree is allowed, just as רבינא said.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (support)
A barren tree, one with no fruit

steps.whatToRemember: Cutting a fruit tree is forbidden while it still gives enough fruit (a קב for a palm, a רובע for an olive), but it is allowed when the wood is worth more than the fruit.

phrases.english: It was also taught so:
"Only the tree that you know"
phrases.notes: דברים 20:20

phrases.english: – this is a fruit tree,
"that it is not a food tree"
– this is a barren tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבינא's exception in step 26 from a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבינא's rule that a fruit tree may sometimes be cut down.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading 'רק עץ אשר תדע' (דברים 20:20) as referring to a fruit tree.

steps.title: Why mention a barren tree if every tree is included?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks: if in the end every type of tree may be cut down, what does the phrase 'כי לא עץ מאכל' teach?
steps.simpleTranslation: But since we will end up including every kind of tree, why does the פסוק say 'that it is not a food tree'?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא challenges itself. If every tree may be cut down in the end, the words about a non-fruit tree seem to add nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 27 read 'כי לא עץ מאכל' as talking about a barren tree. But the ברייתא goes on to include all trees, even fruit trees, when there is a need during a siege. If fruit trees are allowed anyway, a separate phrase allowing barren trees looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: everything, here meaning every kind of tree
what is the פסוק teaching by saying this?

phrases.english: But since
we will ultimately include everything,
phrases.notes: The letter נ in square brackets is the corrected wording, so read it as סופנו, 'we will end up.' He means every kind of tree.

phrases.english: what does the verse teach by saying
"that it is not a food tree"?
phrases.notes: דברים 20:20

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר שֶׁסּוֹפֵנוּ לְרַבּוֹת כׇּל דָּבָר מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from step 27 and questions why one of the phrases it explained is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the phrase 'כי לא עץ מאכל' in the פסוק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If every tree, including fruit trees, may be cut down in the end, a phrase that allows only barren trees seems to teach nothing.

steps.title: Cut down barren trees first
steps.stepSummary: The phrase teaches priority: a barren tree should be cut down before a fruit tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us to cut down a barren tree before a fruit tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its question. The phrase is not about which trees are allowed. It is about which tree to cut first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both kinds of trees may be cut down. But the פסוק still sets an order: use the barren tree first, and touch a fruit tree only when needed. So the phrase is not extra. It adds a rule of priority.

keyTerms.meaning: to put first / to give priority
a barren tree that does not produce fruit
food, here meaning a fruit tree

steps.whatToRemember: All trees may be cut down when there is a need during a siege, but a barren tree comes first. A fruit tree is cut only after that.
steps.whyThisMatters: This fits the theme of the whole section: the תורה protects fruit trees. Even where cutting them is allowed, they come last.

phrases.english: To give a barren tree precedence over a food tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the phrase a new job: a rule of priority instead of permission.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase seemed to be about which trees may be cut at all, which would make it unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase sets an order: cut barren trees before fruit trees.
